discovery: Quantum cryptography: quantum key distribution and entanglement-based secure communication

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, USA

nominees.name: Artur Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) showed that the quantum properties of single photons (no-cloning, and the disturbance that measurement causes) can guarantee that a secret key is secure, with that security resting on the laws of physics. Ekert (1991) connected this idea to entanglement and the violation of Bell inequalities. The Bell test, first a question about the foundations of quantum mechanics, became a working check that a channel is secure. This led to the device-independent protocols later confirmed in loophole-free experiments. Their work began the second quantum revolution: it turned entanglement and single-particle control from ideas debated in the lab into a new physical resource for technology. Quantum key distribution has since been shown over optical fibre networks and satellite links. It has also created quantum communication as a field and helped drive the growth of quantum information science. This is a clear case of basic physics becoming a practical tool.
